decisions.action: Flagged department 'missing' (21) and aisles 'missing' (100) / 'other' (6) as placeholders instead of deleting them.
decisions.reason: They are unknown-category buckets, not real shelves. Dropping them would silently delete real transactions; keeping them unflagged would let an 'unknown' bucket win a 'top category' ranking.
decisions.impact: 1 department + 2 aisle rows flagged; 0 rows removed.

decisions.action: Trimmed/collapsed whitespace in product names (4 rows had stray whitespace).
decisions.reason: Whitespace variants create false distinct products when names are grouped or matched.

decisions.action: Created product_uid: product_ids that share an identical name *within the same aisle* now map to one analytical product (111 groups, 112 secondary SKUs folded in). product_id is kept untouched.
decisions.reason: e.g. 'BBQ Sauce' (2691) and 'Bbq Sauce' (43288) are the same shelf item listed twice; left split they halve that product's purchase volume and reorder rate. Same-name products in DIFFERENT aisles are left separate because they may genuinely differ.
decisions.impact: 112 of 49,688 products (0.23%) re-pointed; catalogue row count unchanged.

decisions.action: Flagged the 3 catalogue products that were never purchased; kept them.
decisions.reason: They are valid catalogue entries with zero demand - an assortment finding in its own right, not dirty data.

decisions.action: Kept all 206,209 nulls as nulls and added is_first_order; no imputation, no row dropped.
decisions.reason: Null here means 'this customer had no previous order' - a real business state. Every single null sits on order_number = 1 (verified), so imputing 0 would invent same-day repeat behaviour and imputing the mean would invent a fake interval.
decisions.impact: 206,209 rows (6.0%) retained with a null interval + explicit flag.

decisions.action: Flagged the 369,323 orders (10.8%) recorded at exactly 30 days as right-censored rather than treating 30 as a true interval.
decisions.reason: The field is capped at 30 by Instacart, so '30' means 'at least 30 days'. Averaging it as a literal 30 understates the real gap for lapsed customers.
decisions.impact: Mean interval is reported both raw and excluding the cap.

decisions.action: Added readable labels assuming 0 = Saturday, and flagged that assumption.
decisions.reason: The Instacart release documents order_dow only as 0-6 with no weekday mapping. Days 0 and 1 carry the volume peak, which is weekend-shaped, so 0=Sat is the standard reading - but no conclusion in this report depends on the names, only on the relative pattern.
decisions.impact: Labels are presentational; all day-level findings are also stated by day number.

decisions.action: Verified order_dow in 0-6, order_hour_of_day in 0-23, order_number >= 1; no invalid values found.
decisions.reason: Range checks before any time analysis, so a bad code value cannot be read as a real behavioural pattern.

decisions.action: Noted order_number maxes out at exactly 100 and left it as is.
decisions.reason: A clean ceiling at a round number is a collection cap, not a coincidence: the most loyal customers' histories are truncated.
decisions.impact: Affects the top of the order-frequency distribution only; stated wherever it matters.

decisions.action: Stacked order_products__prior (32,434,489 lines) and order_products__train (1,384,617 lines) into one 33,819,106-line basket table, keeping a source column.
decisions.reason: Both files have real basket contents and identical schemas; train is simply each selected customer's most recent order. Analysing only prior would throw away 1.38M real purchase lines. The 75,000 test orders have no contents at all, so they can never enter item-level analysis.

decisions.action: Verified (order_id, product_id) is unique, reordered is strictly 0/1, add_to_cart_order >= 1; nothing to clean.
decisions.reason: The grain must be one line per product per order before any basket-size or reorder-rate maths.

join_log.reason: Left join keyed on the product PK so no basket line can be lost. Every product_id resolved (0 orphans), so the row count is unchanged - which is the test that the join is a true many-to-one.

join_log.right: orders (-> user_id, order_number, dow, hour, days_since_prior)
join_log.reason: Same shape of join on the order PK. Row count again unchanged, confirming every basket line belongs to exactly one known order and no fan-out occurred.

Aggregate FIRST, then left join: joining the line-level table directly would multiply the 3.42M order rows into 33.8M and break every order-level average. Left (not inner) keeps the 75,000 test orders, whose basket_size is legitimately null.
